sql-high-balance-checking.title: High-Balance Checking Accounts
sql-high-balance-checking.description:
The bank's relationship managers want to phone every customer who keeps a lot of money in a
**checking** account, so they can pitch a money-market product.

**Table** (dataset `bank`):

- `account(account_id, product_cd, cust_id, open_date, close_date, last_activity_date, status, open_branch_id, open_emp_id, avail_balance, pending_balance)`

Return every account where

- `product_cd` is `'CHK'`,
- `status` is `'ACTIVE'`, and
- `avail_balance` is **strictly greater than 5000**.

**Columns, in this order:** `account_id`, `cust_id`, `avail_balance`

**Order:** by `avail_balance` from highest to lowest.
sql-high-balance-checking.solution:
SELECT account_id, cust_id, avail_balance
FROM account
WHERE product_cd = 'CHK'
  AND status = 'ACTIVE'
  AND avail_balance > 5000
ORDER BY avail_balance DESC;

guide.prereqs: SELECT / FROM / WHERE / ORDER BY (modules *Query primer* and *Filtering*).
guide.intuition: Three independent conditions must all hold, so they are joined with `AND`. Sorting is a separate, final step.
hints: Start with `SELECT account_id, cust_id, avail_balance FROM account`.
Each requirement becomes one predicate; combine them with AND.
`ORDER BY avail_balance DESC` puts the biggest balances first.
guide.brute_force: There is nothing slower to compare against: a single table scan with a filter is the whole job.
guide.approach:
1. `FROM account` - one table, no joins.
2. `WHERE product_cd = 'CHK' AND status = 'ACTIVE' AND avail_balance > 5000` - every row must pass all three tests.
3. Project only the three requested columns.
4. `ORDER BY avail_balance DESC`.

Dry run: an account with `CHK / ACTIVE / 7893.71` passes; `CHK / FROZEN / 9000` fails the status test; `SAV / ACTIVE / 8000` fails the product test.
guide.complexity: One pass over `account` (O(n)). An index on `(product_cd, status)` would let the engine skip non-checking rows - try `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` after creating one.
guide.pitfalls:
- `> 5000` versus `>= 5000`: the task says *strictly greater*.
- String literals use **single** quotes. In standard SQL `"CHK"` is an *identifier*; SQLite only falls back to treating it as a string, which hides bugs.
- Forgetting `DESC` returns the smallest balances first.
guide.follow_up: Add `LIMIT 5` to call only the top five, or filter on `pending_balance` too.

sql-incomplete-customer-profiles.title: Incomplete Customer Profiles
sql-incomplete-customer-profiles.description:
The CRM team is cleaning up the shop's customer list. A profile is *incomplete* when its
`email` **or** its `city` is missing (`NULL`).

**Table** (dataset `shop`):

- `customers(customer_id, first_name, last_name, email, city, country, signup_date, referred_by)`

**Columns, in this order:** `customer_id`, `first_name`, `last_name`, `country`

**Order:** by `customer_id` ascending.
sql-incomplete-customer-profiles.solution:
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, country
FROM customers
WHERE email IS NULL OR city IS NULL
ORDER BY customer_id;

guide.prereqs: NULL and three-valued logic (lesson *NULL: the four-letter word*).
guide.intuition: A missing value is not equal to anything - not even to another missing value - so `= NULL` never matches. SQL gives you a dedicated test: `IS NULL`.
hints: Try `WHERE email = NULL` and notice that it returns nothing. Why?
Use `IS NULL` for each column.
Either missing column qualifies, so combine with OR.
guide.approach:
`WHERE email IS NULL OR city IS NULL` keeps a row if at least one of the two columns is missing.
Because `IS NULL` always returns TRUE or FALSE (never UNKNOWN), the OR behaves exactly as in ordinary logic.
guide.complexity: A full scan of `customers`; fine for any table that fits in a dashboard query.
guide.pitfalls:
- `email = NULL` evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row, and WHERE drops UNKNOWN rows - you get an empty result and no error.
- An empty string `''` is **not** NULL (except in Oracle). If your data mixes both, test `COALESCE(email, '') = ''`.
guide.follow_up: Count incomplete profiles per country with GROUP BY.

sql-account-owners.title: Who Owns Each Account?
sql-account-owners.description:
List every account that belongs to an **individual** (person) customer together with the owner's
name and the product's descriptive name.

**Tables** (dataset `bank`):

- `account(account_id, product_cd, cust_id, ..., status, avail_balance, ...)`
- `individual(cust_id, fname, lname, birth_date)` - one row per person customer
- `product(product_cd, name, product_type_cd, date_offered, date_retired)`

**Columns, in this order:** `account_id`, `fname`, `lname`, `product_name`
(the `product.name` column, aliased).

Any row order is accepted.
sql-account-owners.solution:
SELECT a.account_id, i.fname, i.lname, p.name AS product_name
FROM account a
JOIN individual i ON i.cust_id = a.cust_id
JOIN product p    ON p.product_cd = a.product_cd;

guide.prereqs: Inner joins and table aliases (module *Querying multiple tables*).
guide.intuition: `account` holds foreign keys (`cust_id`, `product_cd`); each JOIN follows one key to the table that holds the descriptive data.
hints: Join `account` to `individual` on `cust_id`.
Join to `product` on `product_cd`.
Business customers have no row in `individual`, so an INNER JOIN drops their accounts automatically.
guide.approach:
Three-table inner join. The order you write the joins in does not matter to the result; the optimizer chooses its own join order.

Alias the tables (`a`, `i`, `p`) so the ON clauses stay readable, and alias `p.name` as `product_name` because the task asks for that column name.
guide.complexity: With primary keys on `individual.cust_id` and `product.product_cd`, each account row costs two index lookups: O(n log m).
guide.pitfalls:
- Joining `customer` instead of `individual` gives no names - names live in the subtype tables.
- Omitting an ON condition (old comma syntax without a WHERE) produces a Cartesian product.
- `name` is ambiguous across tables; always qualify it.

sql-employees-senior-to-boss.title: Employees Who Joined Before Their Boss
sql-employees-senior-to-boss.description:
Each employee row stores the id of its manager in `superior_emp_id`. Find the employees who were
hired **before** their own manager (an earlier `start_date`).

**Table** (dataset `bank`):

- `employee(emp_id, fname, lname, start_date, end_date, superior_emp_id, dept_id, title, assigned_branch_id)`

**Columns, in this order:**
`emp_id`, `employee` (first and last name separated by one space), `employee_start`,
`manager` (same format), `manager_start`

**Order:** by `emp_id`.
sql-employees-senior-to-boss.solution:
SELECT e.emp_id,
       e.fname || ' ' || e.lname AS employee,
       e.start_date              AS employee_start,
       m.fname || ' ' || m.lname AS manager,
       m.start_date              AS manager_start
FROM employee e
JOIN employee m ON m.emp_id = e.superior_emp_id
WHERE e.start_date < m.start_date
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

guide.prereqs: Self joins (lesson *Multi-table and self joins*), string concatenation with `||`.
guide.intuition: Treat the one `employee` table as two copies: one playing *worker*, one playing *manager*. Aliases make that possible.
hints: `FROM employee e JOIN employee m ON m.emp_id = e.superior_emp_id`.
Compare `e.start_date` with `m.start_date`.
Concatenate names with `||` (standard SQL; MySQL uses CONCAT).
guide.approach: Self-join on the manager key, filter on the date comparison, build the display names, sort.
guide.complexity: Each employee looks up its manager by primary key: O(n log n) at worst.
guide.pitfalls:
- Reversing the ON condition (`e.emp_id = m.superior_emp_id`) pairs managers with their *reports*, flipping the meaning.
- The president has `superior_emp_id = NULL`, so an inner join drops her - correct here, because she has no boss.
- In MySQL `||` is logical OR by default; use `CONCAT(e.fname, ' ', e.lname)`.

sql-cross-branch-transactions.title: Transactions Away From Home
sql-cross-branch-transactions.description:
A transaction is *away from home* when it was executed at a branch different from the branch where
its account was opened. Report such transactions with both branch names.

**Tables** (dataset `bank`):

- `txn(txn_id, txn_date, account_id, txn_type_cd, amount, teller_emp_id, execution_branch_id, funds_avail_date)`
  (`execution_branch_id` is NULL for ATM/online transactions - ignore those)
- `account(account_id, ..., open_branch_id, ...)`
- `branch(branch_id, name, address, city, state, zip)`

**Columns, in this order:** `txn_id`, `account_id`, `home_branch`, `executed_at`
(the two branch **names**)

Any row order is accepted.
sql-cross-branch-transactions.solution:
SELECT t.txn_id, t.account_id,
       hb.name AS home_branch,
       xb.name AS executed_at
FROM txn t
JOIN account a ON a.account_id = t.account_id
JOIN branch hb ON hb.branch_id = a.open_branch_id
JOIN branch xb ON xb.branch_id = t.execution_branch_id
WHERE t.execution_branch_id <> a.open_branch_id;

guide.prereqs: Joining the same table twice (lesson *Multi-table and self joins*).
guide.intuition: You need two different branch rows per transaction, so `branch` appears twice under two aliases - one per role.
hints: Join `txn` to `account` to learn the home branch id.
Join `branch` once as `hb` (home) and once as `xb` (executed).
Filter where the two ids differ.
guide.approach:
1. `txn t JOIN account a` - get `open_branch_id`.
2. `JOIN branch hb ON hb.branch_id = a.open_branch_id`.
3. `JOIN branch xb ON xb.branch_id = t.execution_branch_id` - this inner join also discards ATM rows whose branch is NULL.
4. `WHERE t.execution_branch_id <> a.open_branch_id`.
guide.complexity: Three primary-key lookups per transaction: O(n log m).
guide.pitfalls:
- Using one alias for `branch` forces both ids to match the same row, which returns nothing useful.
- `NULL <> 2` is UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so ATM rows vanish from the WHERE anyway - but be deliberate about it.
guide.follow_up: Count away-from-home transactions per executing branch.

sql-branch-cities-with-customers.title: Cities With Both Branches and Customers
sql-branch-cities-with-customers.description:
Which cities host at least one bank **branch** and are also home to at least one **customer**?

**Tables** (dataset `bank`):

- `branch(branch_id, name, address, city, state, zip)`
- `customer(cust_id, fed_id, cust_type_cd, address, city, state, postal_code)`

**Columns:** `city`

**Order:** alphabetical.

Solve it with a **set operator** rather than a join.
sql-branch-cities-with-customers.solution:
SELECT city FROM branch
INTERSECT
SELECT city FROM customer
ORDER BY city;

guide.prereqs: UNION / INTERSECT / EXCEPT (module *Working with sets*).
guide.intuition: Build two sets of city names and keep the overlap. INTERSECT also removes duplicates for you.
hints: Write each SELECT separately first.
Both queries must return the same number of columns.
ORDER BY goes once, at the very end of the compound query.
guide.approach: `SELECT city FROM branch INTERSECT SELECT city FROM customer ORDER BY city`.
guide.complexity: Both inputs are de-duplicated (sort or hash), then merged: O(n log n).
guide.pitfalls:
- Placing ORDER BY inside the first SELECT is a syntax error in SQLite and PostgreSQL.
- MySQL only added INTERSECT and EXCEPT in 8.0.31; older versions need `WHERE city IN (SELECT ...)`.
- A join version needs DISTINCT, or a city with five customers appears five times.

sql-import-email-domains.title: Email Domains in the Import File
sql-import-email-domains.description:
The `customer_imports` table is a messy marketing upload: some emails are in UPPER case and some have
a leading space. Normalise each email with `lower(trim(email))`, extract the **domain** (everything
after the `@`), and count the imported rows per domain.

**Table** (dataset `shop`):

- `customer_imports(import_id, email, full_name, source, imported_at)`

**Columns, in this order:** `domain`, `imports`

**Order:** by `imports` descending, then `domain` ascending.
sql-import-email-domains.solution:
SELECT substr(lower(trim(email)), instr(lower(trim(email)), '@') + 1) AS domain,
       COUNT(*) AS imports
FROM customer_imports
GROUP BY domain
ORDER BY imports DESC, domain;

guide.prereqs: String functions (lesson *Strings and numbers*), GROUP BY.
guide.intuition: Clean first, then cut: once the text is lower-case and trimmed, the domain starts one character after the position of `@`.
hints: `instr(s, '@')` returns the 1-based position of `@`.
`substr(s, start)` with no length returns the rest of the string.
You may GROUP BY the alias in SQLite, MySQL and PostgreSQL.
guide.approach:
`substr(clean, instr(clean, '@') + 1)` where `clean = lower(trim(email))`, then `GROUP BY domain` and `COUNT(*)`.

A CTE keeps it tidy:
```sql
WITH c AS (SELECT lower(trim(email)) AS e FROM customer_imports)
SELECT substr(e, instr(e,'@')+1) AS domain, COUNT(*) AS imports
FROM c GROUP BY domain ORDER BY imports DESC, domain;
```
guide.complexity: One scan plus a hash/sort aggregate.
guide.pitfalls:
- Without `lower`, `EXAMPLE.COM` and `example.com` become two groups.
- MySQL: `SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1)`; PostgreSQL: `split_part(email, '@', 2)`.
- `instr` returns 0 when the character is missing; guard with a WHERE if data might lack `@`.

sql-monthly-credits-debits.title: Monthly Credits and Debits
sql-monthly-credits-debits.description:
Finance wants a 2024 cash-flow summary by month.

**Table** (dataset `bank`):

- `txn(txn_id, txn_date, account_id, txn_type_cd, amount, teller_emp_id, execution_branch_id, funds_avail_date)`
  - `txn_type_cd` is `'CDT'` (credit / money in) or `'DBT'` (debit / money out)
  - `txn_date` is text like `'2024-03-07 14:22:00'`

For every month, return the month as `'YYYY-MM'`, the total credited amount and the total debited
amount, each **rounded to 2 decimals**.

**Columns, in this order:** `month`, `credits`, `debits`

**Order:** by `month`.
sql-monthly-credits-debits.solution:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', txn_date) AS month,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN txn_type_cd = 'CDT' THEN amount ELSE 0 END), 2) AS credits,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN txn_type_cd = 'DBT' THEN amount ELSE 0 END), 2) AS debits
FROM txn
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

guide.prereqs: Date functions (`strftime`), GROUP BY, CASE inside aggregates.
guide.intuition: Bucket every transaction into its month, then add up amounts twice - once counting only credits and once only debits.
hints: `strftime('%Y-%m', txn_date)` gives the month key.
`SUM(CASE WHEN txn_type_cd='CDT' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)` is *selective aggregation*.
Round after summing, not before.
guide.approach: Group by the month expression; compute two conditional sums; round; sort by month (text `YYYY-MM` sorts chronologically).
guide.complexity: One scan + aggregate over 12 groups.
guide.pitfalls:
- Rounding each amount before summing introduces drift.
- MySQL: `DATE_FORMAT(txn_date, '%Y-%m')`; PostgreSQL: `to_char(txn_date, 'YYYY-MM')` or `date_trunc('month', txn_date)`.
- `ELSE 0` matters: without it the CASE yields NULL, which SUM ignores - fine here, but a month with no debits would show NULL instead of 0.
guide.follow_up: Add a `net` column and a running total of net cash flow with a window function.

sql-branch-balance-summary.title: Branch Balance Summary
sql-branch-balance-summary.description:
For each branch, summarise the **active** accounts that were opened there.

**Tables** (dataset `bank`):

- `account(account_id, product_cd, cust_id, open_date, close_date, last_activity_date, status, open_branch_id, open_emp_id, avail_balance, pending_balance)`
- `branch(branch_id, name, address, city, state, zip)`

**Columns, in this order:**
`branch_name`, `num_accounts`, `total_balance` (sum of `avail_balance`, rounded to 2),
`avg_balance` (rounded to 2)

**Order:** by `total_balance` descending.
sql-branch-balance-summary.solution:
SELECT b.name AS branch_name,
       COUNT(*) AS num_accounts,
       ROUND(SUM(a.avail_balance), 2) AS total_balance,
       ROUND(AVG(a.avail_balance), 2) AS avg_balance
FROM account a
JOIN branch b ON b.branch_id = a.open_branch_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY b.branch_id, b.name
ORDER BY total_balance DESC;

guide.prereqs: GROUP BY and aggregate functions (module *Grouping and aggregates*).
guide.intuition: Filter rows first (WHERE), then collapse each branch's rows into one summary row (GROUP BY), then sort the summaries.
hints: Join account to branch to get the name.
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' runs before grouping.
COUNT(*), SUM, AVG all work per group.
guide.approach: Join, filter, `GROUP BY b.branch_id, b.name`, compute three aggregates, round, sort.
guide.complexity: One scan + hash aggregate over 4 groups.
guide.pitfalls:
- Grouping by `name` only is fine here, but grouping by the key (`branch_id`) is safer when names can repeat.
- Selecting a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated is an error in PostgreSQL and in MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY; SQLite silently picks a value from an arbitrary row.
- Filtering on status in HAVING instead of WHERE would fail - status is not a group-level value.

sql-multi-account-customers.title: Customers With Three or More Accounts
sql-multi-account-customers.description:
Find customers who hold **at least three accounts** (any status).

**Table** (dataset `bank`):

- `account(account_id, product_cd, cust_id, ..., status, ..., avail_balance, pending_balance)`

**Columns, in this order:** `cust_id`, `num_accounts`, `total_balance` (sum of `avail_balance`, rounded to 2)

**Order:** by `num_accounts` descending, then `cust_id` ascending.
sql-multi-account-customers.solution:
SELECT cust_id,
       COUNT(*) AS num_accounts,
       ROUND(SUM(avail_balance), 2) AS total_balance
FROM account
GROUP BY cust_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY num_accounts DESC, cust_id;

guide.prereqs: HAVING vs WHERE.
guide.intuition: The condition is about a *group* (how many rows a customer has), so it can only be checked after grouping - that is HAVING's job.
hints: GROUP BY cust_id.
`HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3`.
Two sort keys.
guide.approach: Group by customer, count, keep groups with count >= 3, sort.
guide.complexity: One scan + aggregate.
guide.pitfalls:
- `WHERE COUNT(*) >= 3` is an error: aggregates are not allowed in WHERE.
- PostgreSQL does not allow a SELECT alias inside HAVING (`HAVING num_accounts >= 3`); SQLite and MySQL do. Repeating the aggregate is portable.

sql-category-revenue.title: Revenue by Category
sql-category-revenue.description:
Compute net revenue per product category, counting only **delivered** orders.
Line revenue is `quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount)`.

**Tables** (dataset `shop`):

- `orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, shipping_fee)`
- `order_items(order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price, discount)`
- `products(product_id, name, category_id, price, cost, launched_on, discontinued)`
- `categories(category_id, name, parent_id)`

Return only categories whose revenue exceeds **1000**.

**Columns, in this order:** `category`, `orders` (number of *distinct* delivered orders containing the category), `revenue` (rounded to 2)

**Order:** by `revenue` descending.
sql-category-revenue.solution:
SELECT c.name AS category,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
JOIN categories c   ON c.category_id = p.category_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY c.category_id, c.name
HAVING SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)) > 1000
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

guide.prereqs: Multi-table joins, COUNT(DISTINCT), HAVING.
guide.intuition: Join down to the line-item grain, filter delivered orders, then roll lines up to categories.
hints: The grain after the joins is one row per order line.
An order with two laptop lines would be counted twice by COUNT(*) - use COUNT(DISTINCT order_id).
The > 1000 filter is on an aggregate: HAVING.
guide.approach: Four-table join, WHERE on status, GROUP BY category, aggregate, HAVING, sort.
guide.complexity: Linear in order lines with hash joins; the planner will use the primary keys of the dimension tables.
guide.pitfalls:
- Filtering `status` in HAVING is wrong (and an error in strict engines).
- Forgetting `(1 - discount)` overstates revenue.
- Products sit in leaf categories here (e.g. *Laptops*), not in the top-level *Electronics*; rolling up the hierarchy needs a recursive CTE (see problem *Revenue Rolled Up the Category Tree*).

sql-above-average-checking.title: Accounts Above the Checking Average
sql-above-average-checking.description:
Return all accounts (any product) whose `avail_balance` is greater than the **average balance of
all checking accounts** (`product_cd = 'CHK'`).

**Table** (dataset `bank`):

- `account(account_id, product_cd, cust_id, ..., avail_balance, pending_balance)`

**Columns, in this order:** `account_id`, `product_cd`, `avail_balance`

**Order:** by `avail_balance` descending.
sql-above-average-checking.solution:
SELECT account_id, product_cd, avail_balance
FROM account
WHERE avail_balance > (SELECT AVG(avail_balance)
                       FROM account
                       WHERE product_cd = 'CHK')
ORDER BY avail_balance DESC;

guide.prereqs: Noncorrelated scalar subqueries (module *Subqueries*).
guide.intuition: Compute one number (the checking average) in an inner query, then compare every row with it.
hints: The inner query returns one row and one column.
Put it in parentheses on the right of `>`.
It runs once, independent of the outer row.
guide.approach: `WHERE avail_balance > (SELECT AVG(avail_balance) FROM account WHERE product_cd = 'CHK')`.
guide.complexity: Two scans of `account`: one for the average, one for the filter.
guide.pitfalls:
- `WHERE avail_balance > AVG(avail_balance)` is illegal - aggregates cannot appear in WHERE.
- If the subquery could return several rows you would need ANY/ALL/IN instead of `>`.

sql-customers-never-ordered.title: Customers Who Never Ordered
sql-customers-never-ordered.description:
List customers who have **no orders at all**.

**Tables** (dataset `shop`):

- `customers(customer_id, first_name, last_name, email, city, country, signup_date, referred_by)`
- `orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, shipping_fee)`

**Columns, in this order:** `customer_id`, `first_name`, `last_name`, `signup_date`

**Order:** by `customer_id`.
sql-customers-never-ordered.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.signup_date
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

guide.prereqs: Correlated subqueries and EXISTS.
guide.intuition: For each customer ask a yes/no question: *is there any order for this customer?* Keep the ones answered no.
hints: The subquery refers to `c.customer_id` from the outer query - that makes it correlated.
EXISTS ignores the select list; `SELECT 1` is the convention.
Alternative: LEFT JOIN orders and keep rows where `o.order_id IS NULL`.
guide.approach: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)` - an *anti-join*.
guide.complexity: Engines turn NOT EXISTS into an anti-join; with an index on `orders(customer_id)` each probe is O(log n).
guide.pitfalls:
- `NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` breaks if that column ever contains NULL.
- With LEFT JOIN, test a NOT NULL column of the right table (its primary key), not a nullable one.

sql-latest-order-per-customer.title: Each Customer's Latest Order
sql-latest-order-per-customer.description:
For every customer who has ordered, return their **most recent** order. If a customer placed several
orders on that same latest date, return the one with the **highest `order_id`**.

**Table** (dataset `shop`):

- `orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, shipping_fee)`

**Columns, in this order:** `customer_id`, `order_id`, `order_date`, `status`

Any row order is accepted.
sql-latest-order-per-customer.solution:
SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_id, o.order_date, o.status
FROM orders o
WHERE o.order_id = (SELECT o2.order_id
                    FROM orders o2
                    WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id
                    ORDER BY o2.order_date DESC, o2.order_id DESC
                    LIMIT 1);

guide.prereqs: Correlated subqueries; later, window functions.
guide.intuition: For each order ask: *is this the newest order of its own customer?* The inner query finds that newest order id per outer row.
hints: Correlate on customer_id.
Order the inner query by date then id, both descending, LIMIT 1.
Equivalent window-function version: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1.
guide.brute_force: `WHERE order_date = (SELECT MAX(order_date) ...)` is simpler but returns ties - two rows for a customer with two orders on the same day.
guide.approach: Correlated scalar subquery returning one order_id per customer; keep the outer row whose id matches.
guide.complexity: Naively O(n^2); with an index on `orders(customer_id, order_date)` each probe is a short index range. ROW_NUMBER needs a single sort: O(n log n).
guide.pitfalls:
- The tie rule matters: always add a deterministic tie-breaker.
- LIMIT inside a subquery is fine in SQLite/PostgreSQL/MySQL; SQL Server uses TOP 1.
guide.follow_up: Rewrite with ROW_NUMBER and compare the query plans with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.

sql-pricier-than-category-average.title: Pricier Than Their Category
sql-pricier-than-category-average.description:
Find products whose price is **above the average price of products in the same category**.

**Tables** (dataset `shop`):

- `products(product_id, name, category_id, price, cost, launched_on, discontinued)`
- `categories(category_id, name, parent_id)`

**Columns, in this order:** `product_id`, `product`, `category`, `price`, `category_avg` (rounded to 2)

**Order:** by `category`, then `price` descending.
sql-pricier-than-category-average.solution:
SELECT p.product_id, p.name AS product, c.name AS category, p.price,
       ROUND((SELECT AVG(p2.price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category_id = p.category_id), 2) AS category_avg
FROM products p
JOIN categories c ON c.category_id = p.category_id
WHERE p.price > (SELECT AVG(p2.price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category_id = p.category_id)
ORDER BY category, p.price DESC;

guide.prereqs: Correlated subqueries; derived tables.
guide.intuition: Each product needs *its own* category's average - the subquery is re-evaluated per outer row with that row's category.
hints: Inner: `SELECT AVG(price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category_id = p.category_id`.
Use it in WHERE for the filter and in SELECT for display.
Alternative: join to a derived table `(SELECT category_id, AVG(price) avg_p FROM products GROUP BY category_id)`.
guide.approach:
Derived-table version (often faster, computes each average once):
```sql
SELECT p.product_id, p.name AS product, c.name AS category, p.price, ROUND(a.avg_p,2) AS category_avg
FROM products p
JOIN (SELECT category_id, AVG(price) AS avg_p FROM products GROUP BY category_id) a USING (category_id)
JOIN categories c USING (category_id)
WHERE p.price > a.avg_p
ORDER BY category, p.price DESC;
```
guide.complexity: Correlated: O(n x group size) without an index; derived table: O(n).
guide.pitfalls:
- A category with one product never qualifies (price = its own average).
- Ambiguous `name`: alias both name columns.

sql-employee-transaction-counts.title: Transactions Handled per Employee
sql-employee-transaction-counts.description:
List **every** employee with the number of transactions they handled as teller
(`txn.teller_emp_id`). Employees who handled none must appear with **0**.

**Tables** (dataset `bank`):

- `employee(emp_id, fname, lname, start_date, end_date, superior_emp_id, dept_id, title, assigned_branch_id)`
- `txn(txn_id, txn_date, account_id, txn_type_cd, amount, teller_emp_id, execution_branch_id, funds_avail_date)`

**Columns, in this order:** `emp_id`, `fname`, `lname`, `title`, `txn_count`

**Order:** by `txn_count` descending, then `emp_id`.
sql-employee-transaction-counts.solution:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.fname, e.lname, e.title,
       COUNT(t.txn_id) AS txn_count
FROM employee e
LEFT JOIN txn t ON t.teller_emp_id = e.emp_id
GROUP BY e.emp_id, e.fname, e.lname, e.title
ORDER BY txn_count DESC, e.emp_id;

guide.prereqs: LEFT OUTER JOIN (module *Joins revisited*).
guide.intuition: An inner join would silently drop employees with no transactions. A left join keeps every employee and pads the txn columns with NULL.
hints: `employee e LEFT JOIN txn t ON t.teller_emp_id = e.emp_id`.
`COUNT(t.txn_id)` counts non-NULL values, so padded rows count as 0.
`COUNT(*)` would count the padded row as 1 - wrong.
guide.approach: Left join, group by employee, count a column from the optional side.
guide.complexity: Hash or index-nested-loop join; linear in txn rows.
guide.pitfalls:
- Putting a filter on `t` in the WHERE clause (e.g. `WHERE t.amount > 100`) turns the left join back into an inner join - move it into the ON clause instead.
- COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) is the classic bug here.

sql-country-status-matrix.title: Country x Status Order Matrix
sql-country-status-matrix.description:
Build a complete matrix of **every customer country x every order status that appears in `orders`**,
with the number of orders for each combination - including combinations with **zero** orders.

**Tables** (dataset `shop`):

- `customers(customer_id, first_name, last_name, email, city, country, signup_date, referred_by)`
- `orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, shipping_fee)`

**Columns, in this order:** `country`, `status`, `orders`

**Order:** by `country`, then `status`.
sql-country-status-matrix.solution:
WITH countries AS (SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers),
     statuses  AS (SELECT DISTINCT status FROM orders),
     counts    AS (SELECT c.country, o.status, COUNT(*) AS n
                   FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
                   GROUP BY c.country, o.status)
SELECT k.country, s.status, COALESCE(n.n, 0) AS orders
FROM countries k
CROSS JOIN statuses s
LEFT JOIN counts n ON n.country = k.country AND n.status = s.status
ORDER BY k.country, s.status;

guide.prereqs: CROSS JOIN, LEFT JOIN, COALESCE.
guide.intuition: A plain GROUP BY only produces combinations that exist. To show zeros, first *generate* all combinations (Cartesian product), then attach counts with a left join.
hints: Distinct countries x distinct statuses = the scaffold.
Aggregate the real counts separately.
LEFT JOIN the counts to the scaffold and COALESCE NULL to 0.
guide.approach: Scaffold with CROSS JOIN, fill with LEFT JOIN, default with COALESCE. This *densification* pattern also fills missing dates in time series.
guide.complexity: 7 countries x 5 statuses = 35 scaffold rows; trivial.
guide.pitfalls:
- Joining customers to orders with a LEFT JOIN and grouping still misses statuses that a country never had.
- `COUNT(*)` after a left join would report 1 instead of 0.

sql-experiment-run-outcomes.title: Experiment Run Outcomes
sql-experiment-run-outcomes.description:
For each experiment, pivot its runs by status and compute a success rate.

**Tables** (dataset `mlops`):

- `experiments(experiment_id, name, team, owner, task, created_at)`
- `runs(run_id, experiment_id, ..., status, ...)` with status in `RUNNING`, `FINISHED`, `FAILED`, `KILLED`

**Columns, in this order:**
`experiment`, `total_runs`, `finished`, `failed`, `success_pct`
(`100.0 * finished / total_runs`, rounded to 1)

**Order:** by `success_pct` descending, then `experiment`.
sql-experiment-run-outcomes.solution:
SELECT e.name AS experiment,
       COUNT(*) AS total_runs,
       SUM(CASE WHEN r.status = 'FINISHED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS finished,
       SUM(CASE WHEN r.status = 'FAILED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failed,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN r.status = 'FINISHED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS success_pct
FROM experiments e
JOIN runs r ON r.experiment_id = e.experiment_id
GROUP BY e.experiment_id, e.name
ORDER BY success_pct DESC, experiment;

guide.prereqs: CASE expressions, selective aggregation (module *Conditional logic*).
guide.intuition: `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts the rows meeting `cond` inside each group - it turns row values into columns.
hints: Group by experiment.
One CASE-in-SUM per status column.
Multiply by 100.0 (not 100) to avoid integer division.
guide.approach: Join, group, conditional sums, percentage with a REAL multiplier, round, sort.
guide.complexity: One pass.
guide.pitfalls:
- `100 * finished / total` in SQLite or PostgreSQL is integer division (67/100 -> 0).
- PostgreSQL also offers `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'FINISHED')`.

sql-balance-tiers.title: Balance Tiers
sql-balance-tiers.description:
Classify **deposit** accounts (`product_cd IN ('CHK','SAV','MM','CD')`) into tiers by `avail_balance`:

| tier | rule |
|---|---|
| `low` | balance < 1000 |
| `medium` | 1000 <= balance < 10000 |
| `high` | balance >= 10000 |

Count the accounts in each tier.

**Table** (dataset `bank`): `account(account_id, product_cd, ..., avail_balance, ...)`

**Columns, in this order:** `tier`, `accounts`

**Order:** `low`, `medium`, `high` (a business order, not alphabetical).
sql-balance-tiers.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN avail_balance < 1000 THEN 'low'
            WHEN avail_balance < 10000 THEN 'medium'
            ELSE 'high' END AS tier,
       COUNT(*) AS accounts
FROM account
WHERE product_cd IN ('CHK', 'SAV', 'MM', 'CD')
GROUP BY tier
ORDER BY CASE tier WHEN 'low' THEN 1 WHEN 'medium' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END;

guide.prereqs: Searched and simple CASE.
guide.intuition: A searched CASE evaluates its WHEN branches top to bottom and stops at the first true one, so later branches can assume earlier ones failed.
hints: Order the WHENs from smallest threshold up.
GROUP BY the tier.
A simple CASE in ORDER BY maps labels to sort positions.
guide.approach: CASE to label, GROUP BY label, ORDER BY a CASE that returns 1/2/3.
guide.complexity: One pass.
guide.pitfalls:
- Overlapping ranges are harmless because the first match wins, but gaps (e.g. `< 1000` then `> 1000`) lose rows at exactly 1000 into ELSE.
- Alphabetical order would be high, low, medium.

sql-pending-balance-mismatch.title: Accounts With Uncommitted Funds
sql-pending-balance-mismatch.description:
`pending_balance` includes transactions that are still clearing; `avail_balance` only includes
settled funds. Find accounts where the two differ, and show the difference.

**Table** (dataset `bank`): `account(account_id, product_cd, cust_id, ..., status, ..., avail_balance, pending_balance)`

**Columns, in this order:** `account_id`, `cust_id`, `avail_balance`, `pending_balance`, `diff`
(`pending_balance - avail_balance`, rounded to 2)

**Order:** by the absolute difference descending, then `account_id`.
sql-pending-balance-mismatch.solution:
SELECT account_id, cust_id, avail_balance, pending_balance,
       ROUND(pending_balance - avail_balance, 2) AS diff
FROM account
WHERE pending_balance <> avail_balance
ORDER BY ABS(pending_balance - avail_balance) DESC, account_id;

guide.prereqs: Arithmetic expressions, ABS, ordering by an expression not in the SELECT list.
guide.intuition: These are accounts with work *in flight* - the state a transaction moves between. A real bank updates both balances inside one transaction so readers never see half an update.
hints: `WHERE pending_balance <> avail_balance`.
ORDER BY may use any expression.
ABS gives the magnitude.
guide.approach: Filter on inequality, compute the difference, sort by its magnitude.
guide.complexity: One scan + sort.
guide.pitfalls:
- Comparing floating-point money for exact equality can mislead; real systems use DECIMAL/NUMERIC or integer cents.
- `<>` and `!=` are both accepted; `<>` is the standard spelling.

sql-q1-large-transactions.title: Large Q1 Transactions (Index-Friendly)
sql-q1-large-transactions.description:
Return transactions from the **first quarter of 2024** (1 Jan - 31 Mar, any time of day) whose amount
is at least **3000**. Write the date condition so that an index on `txn_date` could be used
(no functions wrapped around the column).

**Table** (dataset `bank`):
`txn(txn_id, txn_date, account_id, txn_type_cd, amount, teller_emp_id, execution_branch_id, funds_avail_date)`

**Columns, in this order:** `txn_id`, `txn_date`, `account_id`, `txn_type_cd`, `amount`

**Order:** by `txn_date`.
sql-q1-large-transactions.solution:
SELECT txn_id, txn_date, account_id, txn_type_cd, amount
FROM txn
WHERE txn_date >= '2024-01-01' AND txn_date < '2024-04-01'
  AND amount >= 3000
ORDER BY txn_date;

guide.prereqs: B-tree indexes and EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN (module *Indexes and constraints*).
guide.intuition: An index is sorted by the raw column value. A half-open range on the raw column maps to one contiguous slice of the index; `strftime('%m', txn_date)` does not.
hints: Use `>=` on the first day and `<` on the first day *after* the range.
Timestamps carry times, so `<= '2024-03-31'` would miss 31 March afternoons.
Try `CREATE INDEX ix_txn_date ON txn(txn_date);` then `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` your query.
guide.approach: Half-open date range plus the amount filter, then sort. With the index, SQLite reports `SEARCH txn USING INDEX ix_txn_date (txn_date>? AND txn_date<?)` and can even skip the sort.
guide.complexity: With an index: O(log n + k). Without: full scan O(n).
guide.pitfalls:
- `'2024-03-31 15:00:00' <= '2024-03-31'` is FALSE in text comparison - a classic off-by-a-day bug.
- `BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-03-31 23:59:59'` works but is fragile with fractional seconds.

sql-schema-column-counts.title: Schema Inventory
sql-schema-column-counts.description:
Use the database's **metadata** to produce an inventory of the bank schema: for every table, its
number of columns and how many of those columns are declared `NOT NULL`.

In SQLite the catalog is `sqlite_master` (alias `sqlite_schema`) and column details come from the
table-valued function `pragma_table_info(table_name)`, which returns
`(cid, name, type, "notnull", dflt_value, pk)`.

**Columns, in this order:** `table_name`, `columns`, `not_null_columns`

**Order:** by `table_name`.
sql-schema-column-counts.solution:
SELECT m.name AS table_name,
       COUNT(*) AS columns,
       SUM(p."notnull") AS not_null_columns
FROM sqlite_master m
JOIN pragma_table_info(m.name) p
WHERE m.type = 'table'
GROUP BY m.name
ORDER BY m.name;

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Metadata and the data dictionary*.
guide.intuition: The catalog is itself queryable as tables. Joining the list of tables to a per-table column function gives one row per (table, column) - then it is an ordinary GROUP BY.
hints: `SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table'` lists tables.
`pragma_table_info(m.name)` can be joined like a table (a lateral call).
`notnull` is 1 or 0, so SUM counts the NOT NULL columns.
guide.approach: Join sqlite_master to pragma_table_info, group by table, count and sum.
guide.complexity: Reads only the catalog - instant.
guide.pitfalls:
- An `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` column is reported with notnull = 0 even though SQLite never stores NULL in it.
- MySQL/PostgreSQL equivalent: `SELECT table_name, COUNT(*), SUM(CASE WHEN is_nullable='NO' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = ... GROUP BY table_name`.

sql-top2-products-per-category.title: Top Two Products per Category
sql-top2-products-per-category.description:
For every category, find the **two products with the highest net revenue** from **delivered** orders.
Line revenue is `quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount)`. Use `DENSE_RANK`, so products tied on
revenue share a rank (and both are returned).

**Tables** (dataset `shop`):

- `orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, shipping_fee)`
- `order_items(order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price, discount)`
- `products(product_id, name, category_id, price, cost, launched_on, discontinued)`
- `categories(category_id, name, parent_id)`

**Columns, in this order:** `category`, `product`, `revenue` (rounded to 2), `rnk`

**Order:** by `category`, then `rnk`, then `product`.
sql-top2-products-per-category.solution:
WITH rev AS (
  SELECT c.name AS category, p.name AS product,
         SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)) AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  JOIN categories c   ON c.category_id = p.category_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY c.category_id, c.name, p.product_id, p.name
), ranked AS (
  SELECT category, product, revenue,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rnk
  FROM rev
)
SELECT category, product, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue, rnk
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 2
ORDER BY category, rnk, product;

guide.prereqs: Window functions: ranking (module *Analytic functions*), CTEs.
guide.intuition: Aggregate to one row per product, rank products *within* each category with a window, then keep ranks 1-2. The window does not collapse rows, so you need an outer query to filter on it.
hints: Step 1 (CTE): revenue per (category, product).
Step 2: `DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC)`.
Step 3: `WHERE rnk <= 2` in an outer query - window results cannot be referenced in the WHERE of the same SELECT.
guide.brute_force: Correlated count: keep a product when fewer than 2 products in its category have strictly higher revenue. Correct but O(n^2).
guide.approach: Aggregate -> rank -> filter, the canonical top-N-per-group recipe. ROW_NUMBER would return exactly two rows per category (breaking ties arbitrarily); RANK would leave gaps (1,1,3).
guide.complexity: One sort per partition: O(n log n).
guide.pitfalls:
- Filtering `WHERE DENSE_RANK() OVER (...) <= 2` is a syntax error; wrap in a CTE or subquery (some engines offer QUALIFY).
- Rank *after* rounding can create artificial ties; rank the raw value.
- Ranking line items instead of per-product totals ranks the wrong thing.

sql-account-running-balance.title: Running Balance of an Account
sql-account-running-balance.description:
Show the transaction history of account **157** with a running net total. Credits (`'CDT'`) add,
debits (`'DBT'`) subtract.

**Table** (dataset `bank`):
`txn(txn_id, txn_date, account_id, txn_type_cd, amount, teller_emp_id, execution_branch_id, funds_avail_date)`

**Columns, in this order:**
`txn_id`, `txn_date`, `signed_amount` (positive for credits, negative for debits),
`running_total` (cumulative sum of `signed_amount` in date order, rounded to 2)

**Order:** by `txn_date`, then `txn_id`.
sql-account-running-balance.solution:
SELECT txn_id, txn_date,
       CASE txn_type_cd WHEN 'CDT' THEN amount ELSE -amount END AS signed_amount,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE txn_type_cd WHEN 'CDT' THEN amount ELSE -amount END)
             OVER (ORDER BY txn_date, txn_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS running_total
FROM txn
WHERE account_id = 157
ORDER BY txn_date, txn_id;

guide.prereqs: Aggregate window functions and frames.
guide.intuition: `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY t)` adds up x from the first row up to the current row - a running total - while keeping every row.
hints: Sign the amount with a simple CASE.
Wrap the same expression in `SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY txn_date, txn_id ...)`.
Spell out `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`.
guide.approach: Filter one account, compute the signed amount, cumulative SUM over an ordered window.
guide.complexity: Single sort + single pass: O(n log n).
guide.pitfalls:
- With ORDER BY but no frame, the default frame is `RANGE ... CURRENT ROW`, which includes *all peers* with the same sort value - two transactions at the same timestamp would jump together. Adding `txn_id` to the ORDER BY and using ROWS avoids that.
- A self-join running total (`SUM over t2.txn_date <= t1.txn_date`) is O(n^2).

sql-monthly-revenue-growth.title: Month-over-Month Revenue Growth
sql-monthly-revenue-growth.description:
Compute delivered-order revenue per month in 2024 and its growth versus the previous month.
Revenue = `SUM(quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount))` over delivered orders.

**Tables** (dataset `shop`): `orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, shipping_fee)`,
`order_items(order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price, discount)`

**Columns, in this order:**
`month` (`'YYYY-MM'`), `revenue` (rounded to 2), `prev_revenue` (rounded to 2; NULL for the first month),
`growth_pct` (`100 * (revenue - prev) / prev`, rounded to 1; NULL for the first month)

**Order:** by `month`.
sql-monthly-revenue-growth.solution:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS month,
         SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)) AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY month
)
SELECT month,
       ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 2) AS prev_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM m
ORDER BY month;

guide.prereqs: LAG/LEAD (lesson *Offsets: LAG, LEAD and friends*).
guide.intuition: LAG lets a row peek at the previous row's value in a chosen order - exactly *last month* once rows are monthly.
hints: First aggregate to one row per month in a CTE.
`LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)`.
Use a named WINDOW clause to avoid repeating the OVER.
guide.approach: Aggregate, then LAG over months, then compute the percentage. The first month has no predecessor so LAG returns NULL and the arithmetic propagates NULL.
guide.complexity: Tiny: 12 rows after aggregation.
guide.pitfalls:
- Applying LAG before aggregating looks at the previous *order line*, not month.
- Months with zero revenue would be missing entirely; densify with a calendar if that matters.
- Integer division: use 100.0.

sql-best-run-per-experiment.title: Best Run per Experiment
sql-best-run-per-experiment.description:
For each experiment, find the finished run with the **highest `accuracy`** metric. Break ties by the
smaller `run_id`. Experiments with no accuracy metric (e.g. regression tasks) do not appear.

**Tables** (dataset `mlops`):

- `experiments(experiment_id, name, team, owner, task, created_at)`
- `runs(run_id, experiment_id, parent_run_id, run_name, model_type, learning_rate, batch_size, status, started_at, ended_at, gpu_hours, triggered_by)`
- `metrics(run_id, metric_name, step, value)` - long format; accuracy rows have `metric_name = 'accuracy'`

**Columns, in this order:** `experiment`, `run_id`, `model_type`, `accuracy`

**Order:** by `accuracy` descending.
sql-best-run-per-experiment.solution:
WITH acc AS (
  SELECT e.name AS experiment, r.run_id, r.model_type, m.value AS accuracy,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY e.experiment_id ORDER BY m.value DESC, r.run_id) AS rn
  FROM experiments e
  JOIN runs r    ON r.experiment_id = e.experiment_id
  JOIN metrics m ON m.run_id = r.run_id AND m.metric_name = 'accuracy'
  WHERE r.status = 'FINISHED'
)
SELECT experiment, run_id, model_type, accuracy
FROM acc
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY accuracy DESC;

guide.prereqs: ROW_NUMBER and PARTITION BY.
guide.intuition: Number runs within each experiment from best to worst; the run numbered 1 is the winner.
hints: Join runs to metrics with `metric_name = 'accuracy'` in the ON clause.
`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY experiment_id ORDER BY value DESC, run_id)`.
Keep `rn = 1` in an outer query.
guide.approach: Join, number, filter. ROW_NUMBER guarantees exactly one row per experiment because the tie-breaker makes the ordering total.
guide.complexity: Sort within partitions: O(n log n).
guide.pitfalls:
- `SELECT experiment_id, MAX(value), run_id ... GROUP BY experiment_id` returns an arbitrary run_id in SQLite (and is rejected elsewhere) - the *bare column* trap.
- Forgetting the status filter could pick a killed run that logged a partial metric.

sql-latency-moving-average.title: Prediction Latency Moving Average
sql-latency-moving-average.description:
SRE wants a smoothed view of serving latency during **March 2024**. For each day that has predictions,
compute the number of predictions, the day's average `latency_ms`, and a **3-day moving average**
of the daily averages (the current day and the two previous *days that have data*).

**Table** (dataset `mlops`):
`predictions(prediction_id, deployment_id, predicted_at, predicted_label, actual_label, score, latency_ms)`

**Columns, in this order:** `day` (`'YYYY-MM-DD'`), `predictions`, `avg_latency` (rounded to 1),
`ma3_latency` (rounded to 1)

**Order:** by `day`.
sql-latency-moving-average.solution:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT date(predicted_at) AS day, COUNT(*) AS predictions, AVG(latency_ms) AS avg_latency
  FROM predictions
  WHERE predicted_at >= '2024-03-01' AND predicted_at < '2024-04-01'
  GROUP BY day
)
SELECT day, predictions,
       ROUND(avg_latency, 1) AS avg_latency,
       ROUND(AVG(avg_latency) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS ma3_latency
FROM d
ORDER BY day;

guide.prereqs: Window frames (lesson *Aggregate windows and frames*).
guide.intuition: A frame is a sliding sub-window. `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` averages at most three consecutive rows.
hints: Aggregate to one row per day first.
`AVG(avg_latency) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`.
The first day's average uses one row, the second day's two.
guide.approach: Daily aggregate in a CTE, then a framed AVG window.
guide.complexity: Linear after the aggregate sort.
guide.pitfalls:
- ROWS counts rows, not calendar days: if a day is missing, the window reaches further back. For a true calendar window use `RANGE` over a numeric day (e.g. `julianday(day)`) - `RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`.
- Averaging all raw predictions over three days (weighted by volume) is a different metric from averaging daily averages - be explicit about which one the dashboard wants.

sql-overfitting-alerts.title: Overfitting Alerts
sql-overfitting-alerts.description:
A training run shows a warning sign when its **validation loss goes up** from one step to the next.
For every run where that happens at least once, report the **first step** at which `val_loss`
increased, the previous and new values, and the run's model type.

**Tables** (dataset `mlops`):

- `metrics(run_id, metric_name, step, value)` - `metric_name = 'val_loss'` rows, steps 1, 2, 3, ...
- `runs(run_id, experiment_id, parent_run_id, run_name, model_type, ..., status, ...)`

**Columns, in this order:** `run_id`, `model_type`, `step`, `prev_val_loss`, `val_loss`

**Order:** by `run_id`.
sql-overfitting-alerts.solution:
WITH v AS (
  SELECT run_id, step, value AS val_loss,
         LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY run_id ORDER BY step) AS prev_val_loss
  FROM metrics
  WHERE metric_name = 'val_loss'
), ups AS (
  SELECT run_id, step, prev_val_loss, val_loss,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY run_id ORDER BY step) AS k
  FROM v
  WHERE val_loss > prev_val_loss
)
SELECT u.run_id, r.model_type, u.step, u.prev_val_loss, u.val_loss
FROM ups u JOIN runs r ON r.run_id = u.run_id
WHERE u.k = 1
ORDER BY u.run_id;

guide.prereqs: LAG with PARTITION BY; ROW_NUMBER for first-occurrence.
guide.intuition: Compare each step with the previous step *of the same run*; among the increases keep the earliest.
hints: `LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY run_id ORDER BY step)`.
Filter `val_loss > prev_val_loss` in a second step (window results need an outer query).
ROW_NUMBER over the remaining rows picks the first one per run (or use MIN(step) and join back).
guide.approach: Three layers: (1) LAG per run, (2) keep increases and number them, (3) keep number 1 and join to runs for the model type.
guide.complexity: One sort of the val_loss rows by (run_id, step).
guide.pitfalls:
- Without PARTITION BY, step 1 of a run would be compared with the last step of the previous run.
- `prev_val_loss` is NULL at step 1, and `x > NULL` is UNKNOWN - so step 1 is excluded automatically.

sql-org-chart-levels.title: Org Chart Levels
sql-org-chart-levels.description:
Walk the management hierarchy from the president (the employee with no `superior_emp_id`) downward.
For each employee report their **level** (president = 1, direct reports = 2, ...) and the chain of
last names from the top, joined by `' > '` (for example `'Smith > Tyler > Hawthorne'`).

**Table** (dataset `bank`):
`employee(emp_id, fname, lname, start_date, end_date, superior_emp_id, dept_id, title, assigned_branch_id)`

**Columns, in this order:** `emp_id`, `name` (`fname || ' ' || lname`), `title`, `level`, `chain`

**Order:** by `level`, then `emp_id`.
sql-org-chart-levels.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE org(emp_id, name, title, level, chain) AS (
  SELECT emp_id, fname || ' ' || lname, title, 1, lname
  FROM employee
  WHERE superior_emp_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.emp_id, e.fname || ' ' || e.lname, e.title, o.level + 1, o.chain || ' > ' || e.lname
  FROM employee e
  JOIN org o ON e.superior_emp_id = o.emp_id
)
SELECT emp_id, name, title, level, chain
FROM org
ORDER BY level, emp_id;

guide.prereqs: Recursive CTEs (lesson *Recursive CTEs*).
guide.intuition: A recursive CTE is a loop: the *anchor* produces the first generation (the president); the *recursive member* joins the previous generation to its children, until no new rows appear.
hints: Anchor: `WHERE superior_emp_id IS NULL`, level 1, chain = lname.
Recursive step: `JOIN org o ON e.superior_emp_id = o.emp_id`, level + 1, chain extended.
UNION ALL between the two parts.
guide.approach: Standard top-down tree traversal. Each iteration adds one level; the hierarchy here is 5 levels deep.
guide.complexity: Each employee is visited once: O(n) iterations of index lookups.
guide.pitfalls:
- A cycle in the data (A manages B manages A) loops forever with UNION ALL; guard with a depth limit or by checking the chain.
- MySQL requires 8.0+; PostgreSQL and SQLite need the RECURSIVE keyword, SQL Server does not use it.

sql-category-tree-revenue.title: Revenue Rolled Up the Category Tree
sql-category-tree-revenue.description:
Categories form a tree through `parent_id` (e.g. *Electronics > Computers > Laptops*). Products are
attached to any level. Report delivered-order revenue rolled up to each **top-level** category
(categories with `parent_id IS NULL`). Line revenue is `quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount)`.

**Tables** (dataset `shop`):

- `orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, shipping_fee)`
- `order_items(order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price, discount)`
- `products(product_id, name, category_id, price, cost, launched_on, discontinued)`
- `categories(category_id, name, parent_id)`

**Columns, in this order:** `top_category`, `revenue` (rounded to 2)

**Order:** by `revenue` descending.
sql-category-tree-revenue.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE tree(category_id, root_id) AS (
  SELECT category_id, category_id FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.category_id, t.root_id
  FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.category_id
)
SELECT root.name AS top_category,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)), 2) AS revenue
FROM tree t
JOIN categories root ON root.category_id = t.root_id
JOIN products p      ON p.category_id = t.category_id
JOIN order_items oi  ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN orders o        ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY root.category_id, root.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

guide.prereqs: Recursive CTEs; multi-table aggregation.
guide.intuition: First build a lookup *category -> its root*, carrying the root id unchanged down the recursion. Then the problem is an ordinary join + GROUP BY root.
hints: Anchor: each root maps to itself.
Recursive step: a child inherits its parent's root_id.
Join products on the mapped category, then aggregate by root.
guide.approach: Recursive mapping (14 rows), then the usual revenue join, grouped by the root category.
guide.complexity: Recursion is O(categories); the aggregate is linear in order lines.
guide.pitfalls:
- A non-recursive join on `parent_id` handles only one level and misses *Laptops* (two levels below *Electronics*).
- Products attached directly to a root (e.g. *Smart Watch* under *Electronics*) must map to themselves - the anchor handles that.

sql-referral-network-size.title: Referral Network Size
sql-referral-network-size.description:
`customers.referred_by` stores who referred each customer. A customer's **referral network** is
everyone they referred directly, plus everyone those people referred, and so on.

For every customer with a non-empty network, report the number of direct referrals and the total
network size.

**Table** (dataset `shop`):
`customers(customer_id, first_name, last_name, email, city, country, signup_date, referred_by)`

**Columns, in this order:** `customer_id`, `direct_referrals`, `network_size`

**Order:** by `network_size` descending, then `customer_id`.
sql-referral-network-size.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE net(ancestor, member, depth) AS (
  SELECT referred_by, customer_id, 1
  FROM customers
  WHERE referred_by IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n.ancestor, c.customer_id, n.depth + 1
  FROM net n
  JOIN customers c ON c.referred_by = n.member
)
SELECT ancestor AS customer_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN depth = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS direct_referrals,
       COUNT(*) AS network_size
FROM net
GROUP BY ancestor
ORDER BY network_size DESC, customer_id;

guide.prereqs: Recursive CTEs; transitive closure.
guide.intuition: Compute the *transitive closure* of the referral relation: every (ancestor, descendant) pair. Then counting descendants per ancestor is a GROUP BY.
hints: Anchor: every direct pair (referred_by, customer_id) at depth 1.
Recursive step: extend a pair (a, m) with m's own referrals.
Direct referrals are the depth-1 pairs.
guide.approach: Generate all ancestor-descendant pairs with depth, then aggregate. Because each customer has at most one referrer, the graph is a forest and each pair appears once.
guide.complexity: O(total pairs) = O(n x depth).
guide.pitfalls:
- Recursing only from roots and carrying the root id would credit only the top of each chain, not intermediate referrers.
- If the data could contain a cycle, add `WHERE depth < 50` or track visited ids.

sql-longest-login-streak.title: Longest Login Streak
sql-longest-login-streak.description:
The `logins` table has one row per customer per day they logged in (March 2024). A **streak** is a
run of consecutive calendar days. For each customer find the **length of their longest streak** and
the date it started (if several streaks tie for longest, report the earliest one).

**Table** (dataset `shop`): `logins(customer_id, login_date)` - primary key `(customer_id, login_date)`

**Columns, in this order:** `customer_id`, `longest_streak`, `streak_start`

**Order:** by `longest_streak` descending, then `customer_id`.
sql-longest-login-streak.solution:
WITH g AS (
  SELECT customer_id, login_date,
         julianday(login_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY login_date) AS grp
  FROM logins
), islands AS (
  SELECT customer_id, MIN(login_date) AS streak_start, COUNT(*) AS len
  FROM g
  GROUP BY customer_id, grp
), ranked AS (
  SELECT customer_id, streak_start, len,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY len DESC, streak_start) AS rn
  FROM islands
)
SELECT customer_id, len AS longest_streak, streak_start
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY longest_streak DESC, customer_id;

guide.prereqs: ROW_NUMBER; date arithmetic; the gaps-and-islands lesson.
guide.intuition: Inside a run of consecutive days, the date and the row number both go up by 1 each row, so **date minus row number is constant**. That constant labels the island.
hints: `julianday(login_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY login_date)`.
GROUP BY (customer_id, grp): each group is one streak.
Pick the longest streak per customer with another ROW_NUMBER.
guide.brute_force: Self-join each login to the next day and walk chains - messy and O(n^2).
guide.approach:
Dry run for dates 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 March:
row numbers 1..5, day numbers 1,2,3,6,7 -> differences 0,0,0,1,1 -> two islands of lengths 3 and 2.
guide.complexity: Two sorts per customer: O(n log n).
guide.pitfalls:
- Duplicate dates break the trick; DISTINCT first (the primary key prevents them here).
- In PostgreSQL use `login_date - ROW_NUMBER() ... * INTERVAL '1 day'` or `login_date - rn::int`; in MySQL `DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL rn DAY)`.

sql-dedupe-imports.title: Deduplicate the Import File
sql-dedupe-imports.description:
The `customer_imports` table contains the same person several times with differently formatted
emails (upper case, leading spaces). Treat two rows as duplicates when `lower(trim(email))` matches,
and keep only the **earliest** import (`imported_at`) of each person.

**Table** (dataset `shop`): `customer_imports(import_id, email, full_name, source, imported_at)`

**Columns, in this order:** `email` (normalised), `full_name`, `source`, `imported_at`, `copies`
(how many rows shared that normalised email)

**Order:** by `email`.
sql-dedupe-imports.solution:
WITH n AS (
  SELECT lower(trim(email)) AS email, full_name, source, imported_at, import_id,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY lower(trim(email)) ORDER BY imported_at, import_id) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY lower(trim(email))) AS copies
  FROM customer_imports
)
SELECT email, full_name, source, imported_at, copies
FROM n
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY email;

guide.prereqs: ROW_NUMBER, COUNT(*) OVER, string normalisation.
guide.intuition: Normalise the key, number rows inside each key group by time, keep number 1. A windowed COUNT gives the group size without collapsing rows.
hints: Partition by the *normalised* email.
Order by imported_at, with import_id as tie-breaker.
`COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` for copies.
guide.approach: One CTE with two window functions; filter rn = 1. To physically delete duplicates: `DELETE FROM customer_imports WHERE import_id IN (SELECT import_id FROM n WHERE rn > 1)`.
guide.complexity: One sort by (key, time): O(n log n).
guide.pitfalls:
- Partitioning by the raw email leaves ' a@x.com' and 'A@X.COM' as distinct people.
- `GROUP BY email` with `MIN(imported_at)` gives the time but not the matching `source` - the bare-column trap again.

sql-cohort-retention.title: Month-1 Cohort Retention
sql-cohort-retention.description:
Group customers into **cohorts by signup month**. A customer is *retained in month 1* if they placed
at least one order (any status) during the **calendar month right after** their signup month
(for a January signup: any day in February).

**Tables** (dataset `shop`):

- `customers(customer_id, first_name, last_name, email, city, country, signup_date, referred_by)`
- `orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, shipping_fee)`

**Columns, in this order:** `cohort_month` (`'YYYY-MM'`), `cohort_size`, `retained_m1`,
`retention_pct` (`100.0 * retained / size`, rounded to 1)

**Order:** by `cohort_month`.
sql-cohort-retention.solution:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         strftime('%Y-%m', signup_date) AS cohort_month,
         date(signup_date, 'start of month') AS cohort_start
  FROM customers
), retained AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id
  FROM cohort c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  WHERE o.order_date >= date(c.cohort_start, '+1 month')
    AND o.order_date <  date(c.cohort_start, '+2 months')
)
SELECT c.cohort_month,
       COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,
       COUNT(r.customer_id) AS retained_m1,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(r.customer_id) / COUNT(*), 1) AS retention_pct
FROM cohort c
LEFT JOIN retained r ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.cohort_month
ORDER BY c.cohort_month;

guide.prereqs: Date functions, DISTINCT, LEFT JOIN, COUNT(column).
guide.intuition: Two facts per customer: which cohort they belong to, and whether they were active in the following month. Then a grouped ratio.
hints: `date(signup_date, 'start of month')` gives the first day of the signup month.
Month 1 is the half-open range [start + 1 month, start + 2 months).
DISTINCT so a customer with three orders in month 1 counts once; LEFT JOIN so cohorts keep everyone.
guide.approach: Cohort CTE, retained-customer CTE, left join, conditional count. Extending to months 2, 3, ... gives the classic retention triangle (one column per month offset via CASE).
guide.complexity: Linear in orders with an index on `orders(customer_id, order_date)`.
guide.pitfalls:
- Inner join drops cohorts' non-retained customers and inflates the rate to 100%.
- *30 days after signup* and *the next calendar month* are different definitions; state which one you use in an interview.
- PostgreSQL: `date_trunc('month', signup_date) + interval '1 month'`; MySQL: `DATE_ADD(..., INTERVAL 1 MONTH)`.

sql-sessionize-events.title: Sessionize Clickstream Events
sql-sessionize-events.description:
Split each customer's `web_events` into **sessions**: a new session starts at a customer's first
event, and whenever more than **30 minutes** have passed since that customer's previous event.

**Table** (dataset `shop`): `web_events(event_id, customer_id, event_time, event_type, page)`

**Columns, in this order:** `customer_id`, `sessions`, `events`, `avg_events_per_session` (rounded to 2)

**Order:** by `sessions` descending, then `customer_id`.
sql-sessionize-events.solution:
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT customer_id, event_time,
         CASE WHEN LAG(event_time) OVER w IS NULL
                OR (julianday(event_time) - julianday(LAG(event_time) OVER w)) * 1440 > 30
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session
  FROM web_events
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY event_time)
), numbered AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY event_time
                                ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_no
  FROM flagged
)
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_no) AS sessions,
       COUNT(*) AS events,
       ROUND(1.0 * COUNT(*) / COUNT(DISTINCT session_no), 2) AS avg_events_per_session
FROM numbered
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY sessions DESC, customer_id;

guide.prereqs: LAG, running SUM, named WINDOW clause.
guide.intuition: Flag the *start* of each session with a 1 (the gap is large), then a running sum of the flags numbers the sessions 1, 2, 3, ...
hints: Gap in minutes: `(julianday(t) - julianday(LAG(t) OVER w)) * 1440`.
First event of a customer has LAG = NULL - treat it as a new session.
`SUM(flag) OVER (... ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)` assigns session numbers.
guide.approach: Flag -> cumulative sum -> aggregate. This *flag-and-sum* trick is the general tool for grouping consecutive rows by any rule.
guide.complexity: One sort by (customer, time); linear afterwards.
guide.pitfalls:
- `> 30` vs `>= 30` changes the result at exactly 30 minutes; follow the spec.
- Forgetting PARTITION BY lets one customer's events continue another customer's session.

sql-median-order-value.title: Median Order Value by Country
sql-median-order-value.description:
SQLite has no `MEDIAN` function. Compute the **median delivered-order value** per customer country,
where an order's value is `SUM(quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount))` over its items. For an even
number of orders, the median is the average of the two middle values.

**Tables** (dataset `shop`): `customers(customer_id, ..., country, ...)`, `orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, shipping_fee)`,
`order_items(order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price, discount)`

**Columns, in this order:** `country`, `orders`, `median_value` (rounded to 2)

**Order:** by `country`.
sql-median-order-value.solution:
WITH ov AS (
  SELECT o.order_id, c.country,
         SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)) AS v
  FROM orders o
  JOIN customers c    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY o.order_id, c.country
), r AS (
  SELECT country, v,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY v) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY country) AS n
  FROM ov
)
SELECT country, n AS orders, ROUND(AVG(v), 2) AS median_value
FROM r
WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2)
GROUP BY country, n
ORDER BY country;

guide.prereqs: ROW_NUMBER, COUNT(*) OVER, integer division.
guide.intuition: Sort each country's values, number them, and pick the middle position(s). With integer division, `(n+1)/2` and `(n+2)/2` are the same row when n is odd and the two middle rows when n is even.
hints: Aggregate to one row per order first.
Number rows within each country and count the partition.
Average the one or two middle rows.
guide.approach: Dry run, n = 4: (5/2, 6/2) = (2, 3) -> average rows 2 and 3. n = 5: (3, 3) -> row 3.
guide.complexity: One sort per country: O(n log n).
guide.pitfalls:
- PostgreSQL has `percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY v)`; MySQL has neither - use this pattern.
- `AVG` is the mean, not the median; order values are skewed by laptops.

sql-fraud-metric-pivot.title: Pivot Run Metrics
sql-fraud-metric-pivot.description:
`metrics` is stored in **long** format (one row per run x metric x step). Produce a **wide** table for
the experiment named `'fraud-detector'`: one row per finished run with its final `accuracy`, `f1`
and `auc` as columns.

**Tables** (dataset `mlops`):

- `experiments(experiment_id, name, ...)`
- `runs(run_id, experiment_id, ..., model_type, ..., status, ...)`
- `metrics(run_id, metric_name, step, value)`

**Columns, in this order:** `run_id`, `model_type`, `accuracy`, `f1`, `auc`

**Order:** by `auc` descending, then `run_id`.
sql-fraud-metric-pivot.solution:
SELECT r.run_id, r.model_type,
       MAX(CASE WHEN m.metric_name = 'accuracy' THEN m.value END) AS accuracy,
       MAX(CASE WHEN m.metric_name = 'f1'       THEN m.value END) AS f1,
       MAX(CASE WHEN m.metric_name = 'auc'      THEN m.value END) AS auc
FROM experiments e
JOIN runs r    ON r.experiment_id = e.experiment_id
JOIN metrics m ON m.run_id = r.run_id
WHERE e.name = 'fraud-detector' AND r.status = 'FINISHED'
GROUP BY r.run_id, r.model_type
ORDER BY auc DESC, r.run_id;

guide.prereqs: CASE inside aggregates (selective aggregation).
guide.intuition: Group to one row per run; each output column picks out *its* metric with a CASE that is NULL for every other metric, and MAX ignores the NULLs.
hints: GROUP BY run.
`MAX(CASE WHEN metric_name = 'auc' THEN value END)`.
Filter the experiment by name through a join.
guide.approach: Join, filter, group, three CASE-in-MAX columns. The same pattern works in every SQL dialect; SQL Server and Oracle also offer a PIVOT clause.
guide.complexity: Linear in the experiment's metric rows.
guide.pitfalls:
- SUM instead of MAX would add values if a metric were logged at several steps.
- Leaving out GROUP BY gives a single row.

sql-quarterly-partition-summary.title: Quarterly Partition Summary
sql-quarterly-partition-summary.description:
The bank plans to **range-partition** the `txn` table by quarter. Before choosing boundaries, the DBA
wants to see how many rows and how much money each quarterly partition would hold.

**Table** (dataset `bank`): `txn(txn_id, txn_date, account_id, txn_type_cd, amount, ...)`

**Columns, in this order:** `partition_key` (text like `'2024Q1'`), `row_count`, `total_amount` (rounded to 2),
`first_txn`, `last_txn` (min and max `txn_date` in the partition)

**Order:** by `partition_key`.
sql-quarterly-partition-summary.solution:
SELECT strftime('%Y', txn_date) || 'Q' || ((CAST(strftime('%m', txn_date) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3) AS partition_key,
       COUNT(*) AS row_count,
       ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS total_amount,
       MIN(txn_date) AS first_txn,
       MAX(txn_date) AS last_txn
FROM txn
GROUP BY partition_key
ORDER BY partition_key;

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Partitioning and sharding*; date functions; CAST.
guide.intuition: A partition key is just an expression that maps each row to a bucket. Grouping by that expression previews the partitions.
hints: Month number: `CAST(strftime('%m', txn_date) AS INTEGER)`.
Quarter = (month + 2) / 3 with integer division.
Concatenate year, 'Q', quarter.
guide.approach: Build the key expression, group by it, aggregate.
guide.complexity: One scan.
guide.pitfalls:
- Without CAST, `'03' + 2` works in SQLite by coercion but `/ 3` on text is risky elsewhere.
- Very uneven partitions (data skew) defeat the purpose of partitioning; that is what this check reveals.

sql-production-model-accuracy.title: Live Accuracy of Production Models
sql-production-model-accuracy.description:
Build the query behind a *model health* view: for each **production** deployment, compare predictions
with ground truth. Only predictions whose `actual_label` is known (not NULL) count toward accuracy.

**Tables** (dataset `mlops`):

- `models(model_id, name, version, run_id, stage, registered_at)`
- `deployments(deployment_id, model_id, environment, deployed_at, retired_at, replicas)`
- `predictions(prediction_id, deployment_id, predicted_at, predicted_label, actual_label, score, latency_ms)`

**Columns, in this order:** `deployment_id`, `model` (`name || ':v' || version`, e.g. `'fraud-model:v9'`),
`predictions` (all), `labeled` (with known actual), `accuracy_pct`
(`100.0 * correct / labeled`, rounded to 1), `p_label_coverage` (`100.0 * labeled / predictions`, rounded to 1)

**Order:** by `deployment_id`.
sql-production-model-accuracy.solution:
SELECT d.deployment_id,
       m.name || ':v' || m.version AS model,
       COUNT(*) AS predictions,
       COUNT(p.actual_label) AS labeled,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN p.actual_label = p.predicted_label THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / COUNT(p.actual_label), 1) AS accuracy_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(p.actual_label) / COUNT(*), 1) AS p_label_coverage
FROM deployments d
JOIN models m      ON m.model_id = d.model_id
JOIN predictions p ON p.deployment_id = d.deployment_id
WHERE d.environment = 'production'
GROUP BY d.deployment_id, m.name, m.version
ORDER BY d.deployment_id;

guide.prereqs: Views (module *Views and metadata*), COUNT(column) vs COUNT(*), NULL comparisons.
guide.intuition: NULL-aware counting does the heavy lifting: `COUNT(actual_label)` counts labeled rows, and `actual = predicted` is UNKNOWN (so not counted) when the label is missing.
hints: Join deployments -> models and deployments -> predictions.
`COUNT(p.actual_label)` = labeled rows.
Wrap the final query in `CREATE VIEW model_health AS ...` in your own sandbox.
guide.approach: Three-table join, filter production, group per deployment, NULL-aware counts and ratios.
guide.complexity: Linear in predictions.
guide.pitfalls:
- Dividing by COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(actual_label) understates accuracy by treating unlabeled rows as wrong.
- A deployment with zero labeled predictions would divide by zero - SQLite returns NULL; PostgreSQL raises an error, so guard with NULLIF(COUNT(...), 0).

sql-denormalized-order-summary.title: Denormalized Order Summary
sql-denormalized-order-summary.description:
The analytics team wants a wide, **denormalized** reporting table with one row per order, so that
dashboards do not need joins. Produce its contents for orders placed in **December 2024**.

**Tables** (dataset `shop`): `customers`, `orders`, `order_items` (see schema browser)

**Columns, in this order:**
`order_id`, `order_date`, `customer` (`first_name || ' ' || last_name`), `country`, `status`,
`items` (sum of quantities), `subtotal` (sum of `quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount)`, rounded to 2),
`total` (subtotal + `shipping_fee`, rounded to 2)

**Order:** by `order_date`, then `order_id`.
sql-denormalized-order-summary.solution:
SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date,
       c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer,
       c.country, o.status,
       SUM(oi.quantity) AS items,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)), 2) AS subtotal,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)) + o.shipping_fee, 2) AS total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2024-12-01' AND o.order_date < '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY o.order_id, o.order_date, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.country, o.status, o.shipping_fee
ORDER BY o.order_date, o.order_id;

guide.prereqs: Normalization (lesson *Normal forms*), joins, grouping.
guide.intuition: The normalized schema stores each fact once; a reporting table deliberately repeats customer facts on every order row. Build it by joining back and aggregating lines to the order grain.
hints: Join customers and order_items to orders.
GROUP BY every order-level column.
Add `shipping_fee` once per order - *outside* the SUM.
guide.approach: Join, filter the month with a half-open range, aggregate lines per order, compute totals.
guide.complexity: Linear in the month's order lines.
guide.pitfalls:
- `SUM(... + o.shipping_fee)` adds shipping once per *line* - a fan-out bug.
- Denormalized copies go stale when a customer moves country; refresh or accept point-in-time semantics.

sql-post-type-mix.title: Monthly Post Mix
sql-post-type-mix.description:
The content team wants to see how the mix of post formats changes over time. For each calendar month, count the posts of each type, side by side.

**Tables** (dataset `social`):

- `posts(post_id, user_id, created_at, post_type, topic, char_count)` - `post_type` is `text`, `photo`, `video` or `link`; `created_at` is text like `'2024-10-07 18:22:05'`

**Columns, in this order:** `month` (`'YYYY-MM'`), `text_posts`, `photo_posts`, `video_posts`, `link_posts`, `total_posts`

**Order:** by `month`.
sql-post-type-mix.solution:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', created_at) AS month,
       SUM(CASE WHEN post_type = 'text'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS text_posts,
       SUM(CASE WHEN post_type = 'photo' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS photo_posts,
       SUM(CASE WHEN post_type = 'video' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS video_posts,
       SUM(CASE WHEN post_type = 'link'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS link_posts,
       COUNT(*) AS total_posts
FROM posts
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

guide.prereqs: CASE inside aggregates (lesson *CASE patterns*), `strftime`.
guide.intuition: Each output column is a count that only 'sees' one post type. A CASE that yields 1 for the wanted type and 0 otherwise, summed per month, is that count.
hints: Group by the month label `strftime('%Y-%m', created_at)`.
One `SUM(CASE WHEN post_type = '...' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` per type.
`COUNT(*)` gives the row total for the month.
guide.approach: One scan of `posts`: bucket by month, compute four conditional sums and a count, sort by the month label (which sorts chronologically because it is `YYYY-MM`).
guide.pitfalls:
- `COUNT(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts every row, because 0 is not NULL. Use SUM, or COUNT with no ELSE.
- Grouping by a month *name* would merge the same month of different years and sort alphabetically.
- PostgreSQL: `to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-MM')` and `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE post_type = 'text')`.
guide.complexity: Single pass plus a sort of four groups.

sql-users-who-never-posted.title: Lurkers: Users Who Never Posted
sql-users-who-never-posted.description:
Growth wants to email people who signed up but have never published anything. List every user with no posts.
